title: Want a Summer Job? It's Tougher Than Ever for Teens in 2026!
summary: Have you ever tried to find a summer job? This year, it's super tough for teens. There are 219,000 fewer teens working compared to last May. That's a huge drop! Brad Hershbein, an economist, says teens are getting the "short straw" because there are fewer jobs and more competition. Some reasons? AI, rising prices, and even problems with oil tankers far away. Mariella Silva, 19, was lucky to get a job as a barista at Zeke's Coffee in Washington, D.C. She says working makes her feel more grown up. Now, when she wants to buy something, she thinks, "This is like two hours of work!" She even decides to eat at home more to save money. But many bosses don't hire teens because their schedules are tricky with school and sports. Jesse Lauritsen, who runs Zeke's, says if a teen can only work one day a month, it's not worth it. Some cities are trying to help. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, Gayle Hurn hires over 100 teens as lifeguards and swim instructors every summer. She says teens bring joy to the pool and are worth the extra effort to manage. So, if you're looking for a job, don't give up—but know it might take some hustle!
why_it_matters: If you ever want a summer job to buy video games or save money, this article shows that you'll need patience and extra effort, and maybe your city has programs like Ann Arbor's to help.

background_read: In the past, many teenagers worked summer jobs at ice cream shops, pools, or camps. But after the 2008 recession, teen employment dropped because more adults took those jobs.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is now used in some stores for self-checkout and order-taking, which reduces the need for human workers.
Brad Hershbein (an economist who researches jobs for young people) says teens face a 'short straw' in the 2026 job market.
In Ann Arbor, Gayle Hurn (a parks department manager) hires over 100 teens each summer as lifeguards and swim instructors, showing that some places still value young workers.
Article_Structure: WHO: Teens looking for summer jobs, economist Brad Hershbein, and employers like Jesse Lauritsen
WHAT: Teen summer employment dropped by 219,000 compared to last year, making it very hard to find a job
WHERE: Across the U.S., with examples in Washington, D.C. (Zeke's Coffee) and Ann Arbor, Michigan (lifeguard program)
WHY: Because of AI, rising prices, more competition from older workers, and tricky youth schedules, many bosses are reluctant to hire teens

perspectives.description: Teens like Mariella Silva who find jobs feel proud, learn money management, and enjoy being more independent.
Bosses like Jesse Lauritsen find teens' limited availability challenging, which makes it not worth hiring them for just a few hours a month.
People like Gayle Hurn see teens as valuable and worth the extra effort to train, because they bring joy and fill needed lifeguard positions.
